result: Naïve hPSCs share transcriptional and epigenomic signatures with trophoblast cells, including upregulation of trophoblast-associated transcription factors and open chromatin sites shared with placental tissues.
evaluation: Claims C1, C17, C18, and C19 are supported by citations to prior work (Theunissen et al., 2016; Pontis et al., 2019; Petropoulos et al., 2016) establishing that naïve hPSCs express trophoblast markers and share chromatin accessibility with placental tissues. These are well-documented background findings from the literature.

result: Naïve hESCs exhibit significantly enriched expression of trophoblast markers in embryoid bodies compared to primed hESCs, with many markers already elevated prior to EB formation.
evaluation: Claims C20 and C21 are supported by qRT-PCR data (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C) showing elevated expression of ELF5, KRT7, TFAP2C, GATA3, TEAD4, and CDX2 in naïve-derived EBs and naïve hESCs themselves. The data demonstrate enhanced spontaneous trophoblast differentiation potential.

result: Naïve hESCs are unresponsive to BMP4-directed trophoblast differentiation but regain competence after re-priming or capacitation, with capacitated cells differentiating more efficiently than primed hESCs.
evaluation: Claims C22-C24 are supported by experimental data showing naïve hESCs do not survive BMP4 treatment (Figure 1C), but re-primed (Figure 1D,E) and capacitated cells (Figure 1F,G) successfully differentiate with capacitated cells showing enhanced efficiency. This demonstrates state-specific responsiveness to differentiation cues.

result: Naïve hPSCs can directly give rise to self-renewing hTSCs when cultured in hTSC media, acquiring typical hTSC morphology, expressing hTSC markers (ITGA6, EGFR, KRT7, TEAD4, TP63), and losing naïve identity markers, while primed hPSCs fail to acquire hTSC characteristics.
evaluation: Claims C2, C25-C32 are supported by comprehensive morphological, flow cytometry, qRT-PCR, and immunofluorescence data (Figures 2B-G) demonstrating naïve hPSCs transition to hTSCs with appropriate markers and loss of naïve markers (CD75, SUSD2, KLF17), while primed hPSCs do not. Multiple cell lines and passages confirm reproducibility.

result: Primed hPSCs cultured in hTSC media acquire neuroectodermal characteristics rather than trophoblast identity, expressing VIM and PAX6.
evaluation: Claims C33, C49, and C72 are supported by qRT-PCR data (Figure 2H, Figure 4B) showing primed hPSCs upregulate neuroectodermal markers (VIM, PAX6) instead of trophoblast markers when exposed to hTSC media. This demonstrates state-specific lineage restriction.

result: Naïve hTSC derivation is an intrinsic property of the naïve state, independent of specific culture conditions, as demonstrated by similar results from PXGL and 5i/L/A media.
evaluation: Claims C34 and C35 are supported by morphological and molecular data (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G-J) showing naïve hTSCs derived from PXGL-cultured naïve hPSCs closely resemble those from 5i/L/A culture. This demonstrates the robustness of the phenomenon across different naïve culture conditions.

result: Naïve hPSCs can give rise to naïve hTSCs on a clonal level, excluding the possibility that hTSCs arise from pre-existing trophoblast-like cells.
evaluation: Claim C36 is supported by clonal expansion experiments (Figure 2—figure supplement 2) showing single naïve hPSC clones can generate hTSCs with appropriate markers. This demonstrates the differentiation capacity is intrinsic to individual naïve hPSCs rather than a subpopulation.

result: Naïve hTSCs can differentiate into functional extravillous trophoblast (EVT) cells expressing HLA-G and MMP2, with invasive capacity demonstrated by Matrigel invasion assays.
evaluation: Claims C3, C37-C39, and C43 are supported by flow cytometry (90% HLA-G positive, Figure 3C), ELISA, immunofluorescence (Figure 3D), qRT-PCR (Figure 3E), and Matrigel invasion assays (Figure 3F) demonstrating functional EVT differentiation. The data show both molecular markers and functional properties of EVTs.

result: Naïve hTSCs can differentiate into syncytiotrophoblast (STB) cells with characteristic cyst-like morphology, expressing STB markers (hCG, SDC1) and downregulating hTSC marker TEAD4.
evaluation: Claims C40-C42 are supported by morphological observations (Figure 3H), immunofluorescence and qRT-PCR data (Figures 3I-L) showing 3D STB-like cells express hCG and SDC1 while losing TEAD4 expression. This demonstrates bipotent differentiation capacity of naïve-derived hTSCs.

result: RNA-seq analysis reveals naïve hTSCs cluster closely with blastocyst-derived BT5 hTSCs and express key trophoblast markers at comparable or higher levels, demonstrating transcriptional similarity.
evaluation: Claims C44-C47, C6, and C53 are supported by PCA analysis (Figure 4A) showing naïve and BT5 hTSCs cluster together based on cell type rather than genetic background, with PC1 accounting for 41% of variance. Gene expression data (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) confirms comparable marker expression. This validates the authenticity of naïve-derived hTSCs.

result: Naïve hTSCs display strong upregulation of transcripts associated with trophoblast development compared to naïve hPSCs.
evaluation: Claim C48 is supported by differential gene expression analysis (Figure 4B, Supplementary file 1) showing naïve hTSCs upregulate trophoblast-associated genes. This is consistent with successful trophoblast lineage commitment.

result: hTSCs derived from naïve hPSCs correlate most strongly with day 12 post-implantation trophectoderm and poorly with epiblast or primitive endoderm lineages, indicating they acquire features of post-implantation trophectoderm.
evaluation: Claims C50-C52, C7, and C54 are supported by correlation analysis with published scRNA-seq data from human embryos (Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B) showing hTSCs cluster with day 10 and day 12 TE with strongest correlation to day 12 TE. This establishes the developmental stage correspondence of naïve-derived hTSCs.

result: ATAC-seq analysis reveals naïve-derived hTSCs have highly correlated chromatin accessibility profiles with blastocyst-derived hTSCs, indicating similar epigenomic profiles.
evaluation: Claims C55 and C56 are supported by ATAC-seq data (Figure 4F) showing high global correlation of peaks across all three hTSC lines. This demonstrates epigenomic similarity between naïve-derived and blastocyst-derived hTSCs, validating the derivation method.

result: Differentially accessible regions (DARs) analysis reveals naïve hESC-specific sites are enriched at promoters while hTSC-specific DARs are predominantly in intronic and intergenic regions, suggesting importance of distal regulatory elements in hTSC differentiation.
evaluation: Claims C57-C59 are supported by ATAC-seq DAR analysis (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A,B) showing 1,084 naïve hESC promoter DARs versus 208 hTSC promoter DARs, with hTSC DARs enriched in intronic/intergenic regions. The inference about distal regulatory elements is reasonable given the genomic distribution.

result: Promoter regions of hTSC-specific genes are already accessible in naïve hESCs, consistent with prior findings of shared open chromatin with placental tissues.
evaluation: Claim C60 is supported by ATAC-seq analysis (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C) showing only slight increase in promoter accessibility at hTSC-specific genes in naïve hTSCs versus naïve hESCs, and is consistent with prior work (Pontis et al., 2019). This suggests naïve hESCs are epigenetically primed for trophoblast differentiation.

result: Motif enrichment analysis identifies transcription factor binding sites differentially enriched in naïve hESCs (POU5F1:SOX2, KLF4) versus naïve hTSCs (TEAD4, CEBP, GATA, TFAP2 at non-promoters; TFAP2, GATA, SP1, ELK1, GRHL at promoters).
evaluation: Claims C61-C63 are supported by motif enrichment analysis (Figure 4G) identifying distinct transcription factor binding motifs in naïve hESC versus naïve hTSC DARs. The analysis appropriately distinguishes promoter and non-promoter regions and identifies biologically relevant factors.

result: TEAD4 and TFAP2 are known to be expressed in human trophectoderm, while CEBP and GATA factors regulate trophoblast-specific HLA-G expression.
evaluation: Claims C64 and C65 are supported by citations to prior work (Petropoulos et al., 2016; Ferreira et al., 2016) establishing the roles of these transcription factors in trophoblast biology. This provides biological context for the motif enrichment findings.

result: Verteporfin treatment induces widespread cell death during hTSC derivation and in naïve hPSC maintenance.
evaluation: Claims C66 and C67 are supported by experimental observations (Figure 4—figure supplement 2D), but the authors acknowledge the results are ambiguous—Verteporfin could indicate YAP-TEAD4 importance or simply be toxic at the tested concentrations. No dose-response or specificity controls are shown. The interpretation remains uncertain.

result: YAP shows nuclear localization in both naïve hPSCs and hTSCs, and in both trophectoderm and epiblast in human blastocysts, suggesting YAP-TEAD4 may contribute to both lineages in humans unlike in mouse.
evaluation: Claims C68-C70 are supported by immunofluorescence data (Figure 4—figure supplement 2E) and citation to prior work (Qin et al., 2016) showing nuclear YAP in both cell types. The inference about dual roles (C70) is reasonable given the localization data and species differences, though mechanistic validation would strengthen this conclusion.

result: Naïve hPSCs have enhanced, transgene-independent extraembryonic potential that is a distinctive functional attribute of naïve human pluripotency, potentially reflecting co-expression of embryonic and extraembryonic genes in pre-implantation embryos.
evaluation: Claims C71 and C73 are supported by the collective experimental data from EB formation and hTSC derivation experiments, and are consistent with prior work on gene co-expression in embryos (Petropoulos et al., 2016). This represents a major conceptual conclusion about naïve pluripotency properties.

result: Primed hPSCs do not support hTSC derivation but give rise to non-self-renewing cytotrophoblasts in response to BMP4, and fail to acquire hTSC-like morphology in hTSC media.
evaluation: Claims C4, C5, and C27 are supported by experimental data showing primed hPSCs respond to BMP4 (Figure 1) but do not generate self-renewing hTSCs in hTSC media (Figure 2B). This demonstrates state-specific differences in trophoblast differentiation capacity.

result: Other studies have shown naïve hPSCs can give rise to extraembryonic endoderm, and hTSC-like cells can be obtained from expanded potential stem cells or primed hPSCs after CTB transition.
evaluation: Claims C74-C76 are supported by citations to recent work (Linneberg-Agerholm et al., 2019; Gao et al., 2019; Mischler et al., 2019). These provide important context about alternative routes to trophoblast differentiation from different pluripotent states.

result: Primed hPSCs correspond to late post-implantation epiblast with elevated DNA methylation, and BMP4-directed differentiation may produce extraembryonic mesoderm rather than authentic trophoblast, suggesting the protocol is primed-state specific.
evaluation: Claims C77-C81 are supported by citations to prior work establishing primed hPSC characteristics and limitations of BMP4 differentiation (Nakamura et al., 2016; Okae et al., 2018; Bernardo et al., 2011; Horii et al., 2019). The inference about primed-state specificity (C81) is reasonable given naïve hPSC unresponsiveness to BMP4.

result: The derivation of hTSCs from naïve hPSCs presents a novel experimental paradigm to identify early determinants of human trophoblast specification, with TEAD4 playing an important role based on motif enrichment.
evaluation: Claims C82 and C83 are supported by the collective findings of the study, particularly the motif enrichment analysis showing TEAD4 binding sites at hTSC-specific open chromatin regions. This represents a major conceptual advance and identifies candidate regulators for future study.

result: Naïve hPSCs provide a scalable, genetically tractable source for hTSC derivation, with potential applications in patient-specific disease modeling through naïve iPSC reprogramming.
evaluation: Claims C86 and C87 are supported by citations establishing naïve hPSC properties (Yang et al., 2016; Giulitti et al., 2019; Kilens et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2018). Claim C88 is speculative about future applications but is a reasonable inference given the demonstrated capabilities. This represents an important practical implication of the work.

result: Background on pluripotent states: naïve pluripotency corresponds to pre-implantation epiblast, can be captured as mESCs, transitions to primed state after implantation; conventional hESCs represent primed state; naïve hESC culture systems have been developed and used to study developmental mechanisms.
evaluation: Claims C8-C16 provide established background knowledge supported by multiple citations to foundational work in the field. These claims appropriately contextualize the current study within existing knowledge of pluripotent states.

result: The HIPPO/YAP signaling pathway is involved in mouse TE specification, and TFAP2C plays roles in both mouse trophoblast and human naïve pluripotency, indicating species-specific differences.
evaluation: Claims C84 and C85 are supported by citations to prior work (Zhao et al., 2008; Nishioka et al., 2009; Nishioka et al., 2008; Yagi et al., 2007; Pastor et al., 2018) establishing these signaling pathways and transcription factor roles. This provides important context for interpreting the YAP-TEAD4 findings.
